Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-30
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Reed (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Maplebridge Head of ML), Ethan Kim (Infra), Marco Silva (CTO)

Summary:
- Intro to Maplebridge's inference needs and short-term POC goals.
- Primary interest in Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPUs) with VPC isolation; evaluation of warm pool/burst and pre-warm strategies.
- Questions around tenancy/eviction, KMS/encryption, SOC2, failover to hosted model variants, pricing and benchmarking plan.
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to send pricing/security docs and SE to draft benchmark plan; customer to provide traffic telemetry and prompts.

Topics (auto):
- Dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs
- Reserved capacity sizing and burst model
- Isolation and networking (VPC, peering, on-prem path)
- Compliance (SOC 2, KMS, audit logs)

Transcript body (note: automated transcription - some words may be off):
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Jonas our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya: Good thanks, Priya here - sorry for the slight echo, new headset.
[00:10] Marco: Marco - hi. Ethan on my side just joined, hey.
[00:14] Ethan: Hey all.
[00:16] Jonas: Nice to meet you, quick agenda: high level Redwood offering, then dive into Dedicated reserved GPUs, isolation options, prewarm/warm pool and then benchmarks and next steps. Sound ok?
[00:25] Marco: Yep sounds good. We're mostly interested in predictable latency and cost - we run a search+generation layer for clinical summarization, so tail latency matters.
[00:33] Priya: to add, we have spikes during report ingest windows, like 2x-3x for a few hours and occasional traffic bursts after product releases, so burst handling is a must.
[00:44] Maya: Great, thanks. Can you give a quick on your current stack and deployments so we can map it?
[00:49] Priya: Sure - we currently use internal Kubernetes hosted on GCP, model inference today is a mix: smaller models in-prod on k8s with Triton, and we run bigger LLMs on a mixture of self-hosted GPU nodes for nightly batch and an ad-hoc fleet for realtime. It's been... kind of heavy to operate.
[01:06] Ethan: Infra is small team so ops overhead for kernel tuning, quantization recipes etc has been costly. We also have strict data residency rules for PHI so any hosted option needs to be VPC peered or private.
[01:19] Jonas: Makes total sense. So the Dedicated product is essentially a reserved pool of GPUs with your tenancy and VPC connectivity options. You can pick isolation level - fully single-tenant nodes or multi-tenant with tenant fencing. For PHI workloads customers usually choose dedicated nodes in a VPC with our private control plane.
[01:39] Priya: How much isolation is "dedicated"? Is it physical GPU isolation or just scheduler level? We need to know blast radius.
[01:47] Jonas: Good question. We offer two flavors: reserved isolated nodes (physical reservation per customer - single tenant) and dedicated shared nodes (you get reserved capacity but with software tenant isolation). For regulated PHI, we recommend single-tenant reserved GPUs - that prevents noisy neighbor and eliminates multi-tenant kernel sharing.
[02:04] Maya: I want to flag pricing differences - single-tenant reservations are higher per GPU. We'll follow up with the pricing tiers.
[02:10] Marco: Understood. On burst - what are the options if we spike beyond reserved capacity? We can't drop requests during business hours.
[02:18] Jonas: There are a few strategies: 1) Burst pool: short-term burst into a shared overflow pool (higher cost, best-effort), 2) Pre-warmed nodes/hotpool you can keep a small buffer of prewarmed capacity for cold-start-sensitive workloads, 3) Fallback routing to cheaper hosted variants or smaller quantized models to preserve latency at lower cost.
[02:40] Priya: Prewarmed nodes sound interesting - how long to prewarm and what's the memory/KV cache behavior?
[02:46] Jonas: Prewarm depends on model size and tokenizer; for typical 70B-ish we see prewarm times on the order of 30-90s for a full KV cache, but you can keep a hot pool to avoid that. Prewarming keeps KV cache resident in GPU memory - avoids token-by-token cold penalty.
[03:03] Ethan: That cold penalty is what kills us - some earlier tests were 600ms median but cold tail was minutes in worst case.
[03:10] Maya: Right, so the warm pool size and stickiness settings are key knobs - we can propose a warm pool of N nodes for your POC and simulate traffic to size it.
[03:18] Marco: How does eviction work if we keep prewarmed nodes? Do we get charged even when idle?
[03:23] Jonas: If you reserve nodes they are billed regardless of utilization. Warm pool options include ephemeral warm instances that are billed per-minute when active vs reserved capacity which is committed. Typically customers buy reserved baseline for steady state and configure autoscale + burst into per-minute warm capacity for spikes.
[03:40] Priya: Ok makes sense. On networking: we need VPC peering and our KMS for key material - is HSM supported?
[03:49] Jonas: We integrate with customer KMS solutions via customer-managed keys; HSM-backed KMS is supported depending on provider. For private deployments we can support on-prem connectors; for Hosted Dedicated we do VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for encrypting model artifacts and any persisted caches.
[04:05] Ethan: Audit logs and token-level traces - we need them for compliance reviews.
[04:09] Maya: That's part of Redwood Console - per-request tracing, token-level cost/latency, and audit logs that can be exported to your SIEM. We'll include the doc link.
[04:17] Marco: Can we get SOC 2 and pen test reports?
[04:20] Maya: Yes - we'll send SOC 2 summary and our security pack. Full reports under NDA.
[04:25] Priya: Nice. A couple of technical specifics: our average request is 1.2k tokens, peak 2.5k, and about 20 RPS sustained during heavy windows, spikes to 80 RPS for short bursts.
[04:38] Jonas: That's helpful - with token sizes like that we can model throughput. Roughly speaking for that profile you'll want X GPUs for steady state (we'll quantify in follow-up) and a warm pool to handle spikes.
[04:49] Ethan: Also we often do function/tool calling and need streaming responses. Any constraints there?
[04:54] Jonas: Streaming is supported; function-calling payloads are fine. The main consideration is latency SLOs; streaming increases connection stability needs but doesn't materially change GPU sizing.
[05:05] Maya: On fallbacks - many customers use policy-based routing: latency SLO met -> use primary Dedicated model; if capacity constrained or tail latency degraded -> route to smaller quantized replica hosted model or to a fallback queuing with priority. That reduces user-visible errors while controlling cost.
[05:24] Marco: How does model version pinning and rollouts work? We do canary deploys frequently.
[05:29] Jonas: Redwood supports model pinning per-route, canary rollouts and A/B with traffic splitting. For Dedicated you can pin a model version to the reserved pool and run canaries in hosted or separate pools before rolling to Dedicated.
[05:41] Priya: Any restrictions on custom model artifacts and quantization? We run custom finetunes.
[05:46] Jonas: Custom models are supported; for Dedicated we allow you to bring your model artifacts. For quantization we advise a validated quantization profile; we can run quantization/eval as part of onboarding to find a safe config.
[05:58] Ethan: About benchmarking - we want to see real-world numbers for our workload. What do you typically run in a POC?
[06:03] Jonas: For POC we do: 1) ingest sample prompts and payloads, 2) run steady state throughput to agree on baseline RPS/tokens, 3) run spike tests to validate warm pool behavior, 4) measure tail latencies and cost per 1k tokens. We'll prepare a plan with scripts you can run or we can run in a controlled environment.
[06:20] Priya: Can Redwood run benchmarks in our VPC?
[06:22] Jonas: Yes, we can run in your VPC in a Private deployment or via a peered Dedicated environment if network policies allow. For validation we usually do both - internal controlled runs and in-customer VPC runs.
[06:33] Maya: Quick question on procurement timeline - Marco, what's your ideal time to have a POC and decision?
[06:38] Marco: We're aiming for a POC in November and procurement/contract by early Q1. Need exec sign-off by end of year ideally.
[06:45] Maya: Good, sounds doable. We'll aim to have pricing and pilot plan in the next week or two.
[06:50] Priya: Another question - encryption in transit and at rest, plus token-level redaction, is that supported?
[06:56] Jonas: TLS + mTLS supported for in-transit; at-rest encryption via customer-managed keys. For token-level redaction we have hooks and can integrate pre/post processing to strip PHI before telemetry capture - typically done in the customer's VPC layer.
[07:08] Ethan: Are there network egress considerations? We need to track data leaving our VPC to Redwood.
[07:12] Maya: We'll include networking diagrams; for Dedicated peered model data stays in the peered VPC path, logs can be exported to your S3 or SIEM, but yes review egress with your security team.
[07:21] Priya: About SLAs - what uptime and latency guarantees for Dedicated?
[07:25] Jonas: SLA varies by commitment; Dedicated with reserved capacity gets a higher SLA for throughput and an availability SLA for control plane. Exact numbers in the contract - typically 99.9%+ for the Dedicated control plane and quota-backed throughput targets.
[07:38] Marco: If reserved nodes are preempted due to hardware issues, what's the failover story?
[07:43] Jonas: We replicate across availability zones when possible and provide automatic fallback to hosted model variants. For single-tenant on-prem we can also have cold-standby nodes. We'll document RTO/RPO in the SRE runbook for the engagement.
[07:56] Ethan: Ok. On cost - do you do unit economics by token or by GPU-hour? We need to translate into our internal cost model.
[08:03] Maya: For Hosted we do per-token plus per-request metrics; for Dedicated we do committed GPU pricing (monthly/annual) plus overage per-minute warm capacity. We'll send a worked example based on your traffic profile.
[08:16] Priya: Anything about model compilation and kernel selection? We do a lot of variable seq lengths.
[08:22] Jonas: The runtime picks kernels based on architecture and sequence distribution; for variable seq lengths the runtime may use dynamic batching and continuous batching strategies. We'll capture your seq length distribution in the benchmark plan.
[08:33] Marco: How invasive is the onboarding? We have a small infra team.
[08:37] Maya: Onboarding is typically 4-6 weeks: infra setup (VPC peering, KMS), model onboarding and quantization validation, then POC runs and tuning. We can compress phases for pilot.
[08:49] Priya: Good. For the POC scope - we want to test: latency SLO 200-300ms p50 for typical prompts, p95 < 800ms (for interactive flows), and cost under $X per 1k tokens (we'll send target).
[09:02] Jonas: Those are reasonable; p95 under 800ms will guide warm pool sizing and model selection (quantized vs fp16).
[09:09] Ethan: Quick nit - do you support on-prem private deployments for air-gapped environments?
[09:12] Jonas: Yes, Private on-prem package exists; that timeline is longer and licensing differs, but it's an option if you need full air gap.
[09:20] Priya: One more: we have internal compliance that prohibits sending raw transcripts of PHI out of our network — can we configure redaction before logs leave our VPC?
[09:29] Maya: Yes, that is something we've done before - you can set pre-export hooks, or run certain telemetry collectors behind your perimeter. We'll detail options in the security pack.
[09:39] Marco: Ok, so to summarize I'm hearing: reserved GPUs for baseline, small warm pool for spikes, fallback to hosted quantized replica for heavy surge, VPC peering plus KMS integrations, benchmark POC in Nov - is that accurate?
[09:52] Maya: Yep that's it. We'll send pricing, security docs, draft POC plan and suggested warm pool sizing as next artifacts.
[09:58] Priya: One last operational question - how is billing handled for multi-month pilots? Is there monthly billing with credits?
[10:03] Maya: Pilots are usually invoiced monthly or billed to card with a short term commitment; we can structure credits against a signed reserved contract if you convert to committed capacity.
[10:12] Ethan: Great. Any competitors or vendor constraints we should be aware of? We looked at Anthropic and also considered continuing to do everything in-house.
[10:20] Jonas: Yep those tradeoffs come up. Anthropic/other LLM providers can be simpler but less flexible for private deployments; self-hosting gives control but ops cost is heavy. Redwood tries to strike the middle-ground.
[10:33] Marco: Sounds fair. Alright if there are no other questions let's identify owners for the next steps.
[10:39] Priya: I'll pull together the traffic telemetry and prompt examples by next week.
[10:44] Ethan: I'll share infra CIDRs and KMS details.
[10:47] Maya: We'll compile the pricing spreadsheet and security pack and get that over by Friday. Jonas will draft the benchmark plan.
[10:54] Jonas: I'll include sample scripts and payloads and an outline of the warm pool test.
[10:58] Marco: Great thank you all.
[11:00] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and a proposed Nov 10 pilot kickoff.
